Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party

Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years , are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing . China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.

Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that the DPP has not held for nearly three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.

Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.

Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.

Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.

But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.

Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.

Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”

Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.

Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”

Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.

“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

stories.title: Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences
stories.summary: Intel faced pressure to surrender a 10% stake to unlock billions in promised grants.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Intel faced pressure to surrender a 10% stake to unlock billions in promised grants.

The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”

Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”

Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted . “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform . “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”

President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “ convinced ” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

Fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the company’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

It’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official says. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”

Documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

“The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

“It’s just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The company starts making decisions not based on what’s best for the company in the short or long term, what’s best for shareholders, but what’s best for politics and what the government is demanding.”

“That’s not what you want from any company,” he adds. “When you’re talking about the world’s most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that’s a huge problem.”

Representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

The parallels between Nvidia’s government-assisted autogolpe and Intel’s alleged forced sale aren’t exact. In the Intel case, Trump all but accused the company’s boss of being compromised by Beijing; in the Nvidia situation, the president reportedly dismissed concerns from his own intelligence agencies about the executive’s connections to China. But both instances show a growing fusion of private enterprise and public office .

During the Biden administration, Intel won awards for up to $11 billion in government grants and contracts, much of it under the CHIPS Act, which was meant to help build semiconductor manufacturing and assembly plants in America and bolster domestic research.

At the time, there was some grumbling inside the Commerce Department, which administered the CHIPS and Science Act grants, about funding what was seen as a “failing incumbent” in the semiconductor space, says the former official. (Intel had, in recent years, fallen on hard times .) But by March 2025, Intel had received about $2.2 billion of the grants. That’s when President Trump told Congress that the CHIPS Act was “ a horrible, horrible thing .” The rest of Intel’s money was put on hold, tied to hitting certain milestones, while the administration said it was renegotiating the deals.

The same month Lip-Bu Tan was hired as Intel’s new CEO. Soon after, his ties to China made him a Trump target, when Reuters reported that Tan had invested in “hundreds of Chinese tech firms,” some with connections to Beijing’s military. Tan’s former firm, Cadence Design Systems, pleaded guilty to violating US sanctions by selling semiconductor designs to a restricted Chinese military university, and agreed to pay more than $140 million in fines. Tan was never personally charged, but the violations happened while he was the CEO.

Two weeks later, the president was watching Maria Bartiromo’s show on the Fox Business Network. It mentioned a letter a senator had sent Intel about the China ties. Trump posted , “The CEO of INTEL is highly CONFLICTED and must resign, immediately. There is no other solution to this problem.”

Tan went to the Oval Office on August 11 to see if there was, in fact, another solution. He got 40 minutes with the president, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Tan claimed his experience in China was a strength, not a detriment. According to the book Regime Change , Tan argued that there was no way he could’ve known about every one of the deals his many companies made; Trump, who had his own sprawling business empire, surely knew what that was like. Tan promised to give up his holdings in China, according to a letter Tan shared with Intel’s board, and put any proceeds into a blind trust.

“The primary goal was to eliminate any worries about Lip-Bu himself, his Cadence background, and his investments with China,” according to a source with knowledge of the matter. But there were major financial concerns for Intel, too. “We had declining revenues and needed money.”

Neither Tan’s letter, excerpted in the complaint, nor Trump’s social media posts praising the CEO after the meeting mentioned anything about giving the government a chunk of the company. Yet Trump later insisted that a deal had been cooked up right then and there. “He came in, he saw me, we talked for a while. I liked him a lot, I thought he was very good,” the president told The Wall Street Journal. “I said, ‘You know what? I think the United States should be given 10% of Intel.’ And he said, ‘I would consider that.’”

“I should’ve asked for more. It was so easy,” Trump later recalled.

According to the court filing’s review of Intel’s internal documents, Shapiro—a former partner at the New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz—made a verbal offer on August 18. Ultimately, in exchange for the cut of Intel, the Trump administration would free up the $8.9 billion US government grants that it had already won. They wanted about a tenth of the company’s stock for free, in exchange for Washington keeping the commitment it had already made.

Then came the call in which Shapiro insisted there was no room for negotiation. “The board needs to consider,” he said, according to Intel’s summary of his remarks included in the court documents, the “benefits of having a friend in this administration and what the administration can do to help Intel (including with customers).”

Intel’s board met, and decided they hated the deal. “The economic terms that had been proposed [by] the Administration were not, in their current form, attractive to the company,” minutes of the meeting, reprinted in the lawsuit, noted.

But they went ahead with it anyway. Paisner’s lawyers say in the court documents the board took the offer thrust forward by the administration. Intel’s attorneys disagree, arguing in their motion to dismiss that there was some back-and-forth deal-making, and it made the agreement more favorable to the company. The grants became “immediately available” while “strategically aligning the interests of Intel’s stockholders and the US Government.”

On August 25, Lutnick released a video with Tan, sitting side-by-side on cushioned chairs. “I really look forward to have the US government be my shareholder,” Tan turned to Lutnick and said. “And we can work together and make Intel great again.”

Inside the company, the video was “a surprise to everyone,” according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. Some employees joked that it was reminiscent of a “hostage video.”

Not long after that, Nvidia—led by Tan’s friend Jensen Huang—made a $5 billion investment in Intel. “I love seeing their stock price go up, making the USA RICHER, AND RICHER,” Trump posted . “Who would not want to make deals like that?”

Deals, plural. On the day Tan was hauled to the Oval Office, Trump announced that his administration had been negotiating separately with Huang . The Nvidia leader was beyond eager to sell more of his semiconductors to China. “And I said, if I’m going to do that, I want you to pay us as a country something,’” Trump said. They settled on 15 percent of all sales of the H20 model chip. Months after that, they cut a second deal: a 25 percent bounty on sales of Nvidia’s even-more advanced H200 chips.

In their lawsuit against Nvidia, Paisner’s attorneys argue the surcharges amount to “unlawful taxes,” and that the board’s “decisions to enter into such agreements are the product of mismanagement and breaches of fiduciary duty.”

In court, NVIDIA’s lawyers insisted that the company “did not enter into any illegal ‘agreement’ with the government but instead engaged with the government and stated that it would comply with federal regulations.” Moreover, the attorneys say Paisner is trying to make a political point, rather than a legal one. “When asked about his purpose in bringing this action,” they write, “Paisner was candid: ‘It’s to make a public point of how NVIDIA conducts itself.’”

The attorneys wrote this in May, months before Nvidia’s and Huang’s recent drama. Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said on the company’s quarterly earnings call that it did “ not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO ,” citing his “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” (Not to mention mounting evidence that the company’s most sophisticated chips were making their way to China, in violation of US law.) But, according to The New York Times, after days of pressure from top administration officials, the company and the government essentially struck a deal Sunday night to reinstate Huang.

“Don’t think for a second that politics ever play a role in this company, not even a little bit,” Huang said during his first company-wide meeting after rejoining the company, WIRED reported . “We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”

Additional reporting by Lauren Goode .

This story originally appeared on wired.com .

stories.title: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
stories.summary: Other countries have rerouted trade in response to his first tariff salvo, now they are looking beyond Trump's tenure.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China Published 1 day ago

New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause Published 22 hours ago

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow Published 6 days ago

However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".

Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC , external : "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."

The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.

It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.

The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.

Canada has seen flat exports to the USA since tariffs, fewer cars and lumber, but pricier flows of energy. Its exports, especially commodities, to the rest of the world have rocketed.

This means that next month's G20 summit at the president's Miami resort is an important moment. In general US allies have not rocked the boat, accepting the lower level of tariffs as part of the new reality. Could the middle powers choose to upset their host in Florida next month?

The bigger question however, is how much the Democrats decide to keep of the America First trade agenda. It will not be all, but nor will it be nothing. Economists now expect some of these tariffs to stay in place for years.

In a Thanksgiving post, the US president seeks investigation after blue wave of Democrats unseat Republicans

Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.

In a holiday message on social media tinged with bitterness, the US president wished a happy thanksgiving “to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%”.

While revisions to official economic figures are commonplace, Trump has tried time and again to challenge trust in economic data that does not support his claims that a historic boom is underway in the US.

The US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), an agency within the US Department of Commerce, calculates gross domestic product, or GDP, numbers.

“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Thursday. “This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error”.

Trump has repeatedly claimed since taking office in January 2025 that an economic “golden age” is taking hold on his watch. Many Americans have been grappling with a higher cost of living, however – exacerbated by the economic fallout of his war on Iran – and backed Democrats in the midterms.

Trump continued his acerbic well-wishing for “a very Happy Thanksgiving to all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left” as well as “those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work”.

And he revisited another ongoing beef with the news media over his controversial focus on White House renovations and decorations. “I want to commiserate with those reporters and citizens who don’t understand filth, dirt, lack of maintenance, and corruption, and are upset with me because I took time out of my very busy schedule to fix the 17 broken windows, numerous chipped and decaying columns, broken, dilapidated, and missing moldings, and lack of a proper plaster and paint job on the White House.”

The sarcastic intervention continued with a message of thanks to “the murderers, drug dealers, and criminals of all shapes, sizes, and colors” whom he claimed are “mostly gone now”.

“Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from faraway lands,” he concluded. “We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!”

Democratic senator Chuck Schumer, vying to be majority leader in the chamber following his party’s victories in this month’s election took a more conventional approach , wishing “everyone in New York and across America a joyous and restful Thanksgiving holiday with your friends and family”.

Hakeem Jeffries, whom Democrats have nominated to be the first Black speaker in the House of Representatives, also played it straight. “Happy Thanksgiving to everyone in the community and throughout our great country! Grateful for the civil servants on the job who are working through the stormy weather to keep everyone safe,” he posted on X. “May God bless you all.”

stories.title: Government to limit 'abusive lawsuits' aimed at silencing whistleblowers
stories.summary: An MP cited former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed as someone who used legal action to suppress his "appalling abuse".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
MPs heard former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed used legal action to suppress his "appalling abuse"

Published 27 November 2026, 12:54 GMT

A proposed law limiting spurious legal actions or threats to silence abuse victims, whistleblowers and journalists has been backed by the government.

Strategic lawsuits against public participation, known as Slapps, are often brought by wealthy individuals or companies to stifle scrutiny and suppress matters of public interest.

Existing protections only apply to Slapps linked to economic crime, but the government is now supporting a bill tabled by Conservative MP Sir John Whittingdale to extend protections to all forms of public interest reporting

Sir John cited former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed as someone who used legal action to suppress his "appalling abuse of young female employees".

The MP for Maldon told the House of Commons: "That resulted in 27 years in which the information was never publicised."

Hundreds of women have accused Al Fayed of rape, sexual assault and trafficking, after a BBC documentary first publicly detailed the allegations in 2024.

Conservative MP Alicia Kearns said Al Fayed, who died in 2023 aged 94, "turned a culture of abuse and silence into the norm" for women working at Harrods.

The luxury store has previously said it "apologises unreservedly for the sexual abuse inflicted upon survivors by Fayed", and set up a compensation scheme for his victims.

Another example raised by Sir John was journalist Catherine Belton, the author of Putin's People, who faced five lawsuits brought by Russian oligarchs and firms.

Sir John also referenced Eliot Higgins, the founder of investigative website Bellingcat, telling MPs he was sued by Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2021 for his tweets suggesting the Russian mercenary leader was associated with the Wagner Group.

He said: "Prigozhin was already sanctioned in this country because of his association yet nevertheless that case was allowed to proceed."

Measures in Sir John's bill include allowing judges to dismiss abusive claims before they go to trial and to protect defendants from exorbitant legal costs.

Labour's Justice Minister Sarah Sackman said: "No-one should be able to use their wealth or influence to silence legitimate scrutiny."

She added the bill would "strengthen protections against these abusive lawsuits while preserving access to justice for genuine claims, helping defend freedom of expression and support accountability".

The UK Anti-Slaap Coalition said last week it "strongly" supports the bill making progress in Parliament although it voiced concerns over its current wording.

It noted there is an "almost impossibly high threshold" to make use of the early dismissal mechanism and offered to work with Sir John and others to refine the bill.

Sir John acknowledged there are concerns over "hurdles" in the proposed legislation which "could act as a deterrent", adding he expects further talks with the minister.

The Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No.2) Bill was debated in the House of Commons on Friday at second reading.

stories.title: Books, bikes, and The Burbs: These are Ars staff’s holiday gift picks for 2026
stories.summary: We polled the Ars staff about their favorite pickups this year; here's the list.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
We polled the Ars staff about their favorite pickups this year; here’s the list.

The holiday shopping season is upon us, and as is our custom, we’re here with a list of Ars staffers’ favorite recent purchases that could make good gifts. (Or maybe they might be a gift you get yourself!)

Rather than try to write a definitive “best gifts for your sister or brother” type of guide, we simply polled Ars staffers on stuff they’ve actually bought this year that they recommend. The thinking is that if we’re into it, hopefully some of you or your friends or family might be. As such, there’s no rhyme or reason to these selections, really; it’s just a list of stuff we bought that we’re happy about. It’s heavy on interesting books and cycling accessories, but there are some gadgets and the like in here, too.

For each gadget (or whatever else it might be), we have a brief description of how or why we’ve been using this particular thing and why we would recommend it. Our picks are ordered by price, from lowest to highest. Note, though, that the prices of these products are listed as they were when the list was written. Online retailers often adjust prices frequently, especially around Black Friday, so just a heads up: The price might be different by the time you read this.

Also, a callout to the Ars commentariat: If you have your own holiday buying recommendations, feel free to share them. We or some fellow readers might take your advice if you suggest something good! Happy holidays!

Under $100

Dungeon Crawler Carl by Matt Dinniman – $13

I understand the convenience and space-savings that e-readers bring. My 2011 Kindle Touch goes with me everywhere I carry my travel backpack, but I’m still a softy for physical books when I’m sitting at home on a lazy Sunday. What started as something of a fanfic send-up of LitRPGs has quickly blossomed into a massive sensation of a series filled with far more depth, heart, and character than the initial premise might indicate. Author Matt Dinniman has an accessible style that will grip any reader with a taste for whimsical adventure. Just be warned that if you leave the books under the tree, you might not see much of the recipient until New Year’s.

– Nick Indge

Undersea War: The Battle to Control the Cables and Pipelines That Connect Our World by Elisabeth Braw – $30

Lightning Beneath the Sea: The Race to Wire the World and the Dawn of the Information Age by James M. Tabor – $32

Two excellent books that help describe how the Internet’s undersea backbone became a globe-spanning reality were published in 2026. Together, they form a great gift pairing for anyone interested in how humanity first achieved near-instantaneous communication across the world’s oceans—and how the first trans-Atlantic telegraph cable paved the way for a global network of subsea data cables that now faces growing risks from geopolitical conflicts.

James Tabor’s Lightning Beneath the Sea dives into the astounding real-life story of how American entrepreneur Cyrus Field, lacking in expertise but driven by personal fervor, set out to achieve peace on Earth by laying a 2,000-mile telegraph cable made of copper across the Atlantic seafloor in 1866.

To pull off the feat, Field managed to convince some of the greatest innovators and scientific luminaries of his day, such as Samuel F.B. Morse, Lord Kelvin, and Michael Faraday, to join his venture. He also refitted the SS Great Eastern steamship, the largest passenger liner ship built to date, as a cable-laying vessel.

That first ocean-spanning telegraph cable gave rise to more such cables for transmitting messages around the world. Eventually copper gave way to a network of subsea fiber-optic cables that became the Internet’s undersea backbone, and the modern world also became interlinked with submarine power cables and underwater pipelines for carrying oil and gas.

But all that undersea infrastructure is now facing growing danger from the threat of deliberate sabotage, as described in Elisabeth Braw’s book Undersea War . Her book provides a sobering but enlightening look at why subsea cables and pipelines are becoming more tempting targets amid rising geopolitical tensions and conflicts—and how governments and companies are responding to recent cable-cutting incidents around the world.

– Jeremy Hsu

Read Ars Technica’s Q&A with Elisabeth Braw about Undersea War .

The Burbs Collector’s Edition 4K Blu-ray – $32

It’s a little-remembered film for most people, but I absolutely love The Burbs . Sure, it’s more Halloween fare than Christmas, but last year I picked The Thing , so clearly “1980s movies for October” is my December viewing MO.

Starring Tom Hanks, Carrie Fisher, and Corey Feldman, this is a dry, hilarious send-up of suburban life with a horror-adjacent mystery that keeps you guessing. (It’s not scary, though.) I hardly ever hear anyone else talk about this movie, but I love it, and it only recently came out in 4K, so I’m taking this opportunity to shout it out.

– Samuel Axon

How Apollo Flew to the Moon by David Woods – $35

If you’re a technically minded Ars reader looking for a nice book to snuggle down with over the holidays, David Woods’ How Apollo Flew to the Moon could be just the thing. (There’s also an audiobook version .) Woods has an accessible style that breaks down complex engineering challenges and their solutions into easily digestible chunks that clarify without oversimplifying. He uses that style to take readers on a detailed trip through the machinery of Project Apollo, from the launch facilities and Mission Control all the way to the specific mechanics of how to navigate to and land on the Moon—and, from there, how to return safely to Earth.

Ever wondered about the insane engineering that let the Saturn V’s first stage burn almost 15 tons of fuel every second as it powered the crew into orbit? Or how to pinpoint a spacecraft’s centimeter-precise distance from Earth on its way to the Moon? Or how Apollo crews tracked their own position with stellar navigation, using sextants and star sightings? Or what a REFSMMAT is, or how television transmissions from the Moon worked, or how they got those crazy lunar buggies onto the Moon’s surface? All these questions and more are given beautifully complete and technically satisfying answers, suitable for both the curious layperson and also the interested engineer. Grab this book and stun your family at Christmas with amazing Apollo trivia—as a bonus, you’ll have the knowledge to make your “We never landed on the Moon!” conspiracy theorist uncle so angry that he stops talking and watches football in grumpy silence! Everyone wins!

– Lee Hutchinson

Final Fantasy Resonance

PS5 – $64

Switch – $50

Steam (Digital) – $50

Xbox (Digital) – $50

As someone who grew up in the classic era of 16-bit SNES RPGs, this 40th anniversary tribute to the series’ history is everything I could have ever wanted in a modern entry. I haven’t properly played through a Final Fantasy entry since the days of Final Fantasy X on PlayStation 2, but when friends kept nudging me that this was the perfect “Nick game,” I figured I should probably take a look. There’s a free six-hour demo available on supported platforms if you’re still on the fence about picking this one up, but don’t be surprised if you end up grabbing a copy for yourself.

– Nick Indge

Govee Star Light Projector (Nebula Effect) – $70

For the past couple of years, I’ve been transforming my tiny office into a sanctuary in the evenings, since I do most of my writing (and gaming) in here then. It started with Govee Hexa panels, then came an RGB TV backlight, then colorful smart bulbs for the built-in light fixtures. I topped it off with the Star Light projector, which coats the ceiling in a soothing, ever-shifting, immersive stars-and-nebula effect.

It’s probably not for everybody, but my office is tiny, and I spend a lot of time here both for work and for fun. Tapping a button to completely shift the vibe is surprisingly effective at making it a room I don’t mind spending time in even after I’ve been working in it all day.

– Samuel Axon

M-Vave FM-1 – $84

Easily my favorite impulse purchase of 2026, the FM-1 is a great gift for curious tinkerers and experienced musicians alike. At around $70 or less, you don’t have to break the bank to get fiddling. A perfectly decent stock synthesizer on its own, the real fun starts when you begin experimenting with the community firmware packages that transform the synth into anything from a multi-track groovebox to one of the more hilarious ways that I’ve ever tried to play Doom .

– Nick Indge

Alan Feeney stepped down from Reform UK after the comments emerged

Published 27 November 2026, 10:57 GMT

Four council seats in the West Midlands have been defended by Reform UK after by-elections triggered by the resignation of a councillor featured in an ITV News undercover investigation , external .

Alan Feeney, who later stepped down from the party , was filmed calling Asian homeowners "parasites", in the run up to council elections in May.

In October, he resigned from every post he held on Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council and Birmingham City Council, adding his remarks "were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable".

On Thursday night, Reform held one seat in Shard End on Birmingham City Council and three seats in Castle Bromwich on Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council.

Sarah Myers was voted in to replace Feeney in Shard End, edging Labour by 104 votes, with Birmingham City Council recording a voter turnout of 19%.

Speaking after her win, she said: "I am delighted to have been elected for Shard End, and I'm excited to get to work delivering for local residents.

"Shard End was a former Labour stronghold, and has been badly let down over decades of neglect.

"I look forward to proving that the confidence residents have in Reform is well placed."

'Patriotic party of good'

A Reform UK Birmingham spokesperson said the results showed the public were "sticking with Reform".

"The good people of Shard End recognise that Reform is a patriotic party of good, hard-working individuals who want to fix our country," they added.

The result means that out of 101 councillors on the city council, Reform has 22, while the Green Party has 19, the Conservatives have 16, Labour has 14, and the Liberal Democrats has 12.

Better Birmingham also has seven councillors, Birmingham Independent Workers' Group has five, there are four independent councillors, and two from the Birmingham Independents Group.

Despite Reform having more councillors, Liberal Democrat Roger Harmer remains city council leader , with his party forming a minority administration with the Greens and the Better Birmingham Group.

In Castle Bromwich, Mark Evans, Jacqueline Sheila Howse and Garry Taylor also gained the most votes for Reform.

The outcome means that out of 51 councillors, Reform has 15 seats.

The largest party is still the Conservatives with 25, who run the authority as a minority administration.

stories.body:
Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’

Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU

Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.

Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

“China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” the Chinese commerce ministry spokesman, He Yadong, said at a regular briefing. “China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”

Brazil was also singled out in the announcement after trade talks stalled.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday that “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.

It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

The Trump administration said that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries. They are being imposed under a law that allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”.

The Trump administration’s new tariff rates would be capped at lower ​levels ‌agreed under ​trade deals ​that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.

The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

Trump met his counterpart, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen last week but the escalation in tariffs will not be a surprise to China, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP news agency.

The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again in Miami on the sidelines of the G20 in December.

“It has become a pattern before every major top leader summit,” Wang said, adding that she did not think the new measures would derail relations between Washington and Beijing.

“Xi has a high incentive to keep bilateral relations stable leading up to the 21st (Communist) party congress in October 2027,”Wang said.

A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Trump andd Xi .

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” said the spokesperson Guo Jiakun.

Greer told CNBC that the administration was proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer said. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”

Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined”, said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”

after newsletter promotion

The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the US to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” said the European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill.

Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.

It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties”.

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.

Taiwan was also earmarked for new tariffs but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech products that account for ​more than 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.

Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the EU, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland and Thailand.

Tokyo’s top government spokesperson, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Singapore’s government said it was “very disappointed” with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidising manufacturing.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will probably support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

However, the Democratic senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos”.

He added: “This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”

stories.body:
Bank of England warns of increases for millions coming off fixed deals over next three years as interest rates rise

Business live – latest updates

More than 400,000 UK homeowners will face a £500-a-month increase in their mortgage payments over the next three years, as rising interest rates heap extra pressure on households, the Bank of England has said.

The Bank’s financial policy committee said on Thursday that out of the 7 million borrowers coming off fixed-rate deals before December 2029, about 6.5 million would have to cough up extra funds to cover their home loan payments.

For about 3.4 million borrowers the monthly increase would be less than £100, while for a further 2.7 million it would be £100-£500. The increase would be even greater for those borrowers coming off much lower interest rates, with about 430,000 likely to see their monthly mortgage payments surge by more than £500.

Warnings about the increases came after policymakers at the Bank of England hiked interest rates from 3.75% to 4% this month. The Bank also hinted at another increase in interest rates to combat inflationary pressure caused by the Iran war. The financial markets have predicted three quarter-point rate rises by summer 2027.

Over the next year, about 1 million households will see their payments rise by almost £200 a month.

The news will put further pressure on Andy Burnham’s efforts to offset cost of living pressures, with the chancellor, John Healey, having used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers .

The figures came a day after the energy regulator for Great Britain raised the cap on household energy bills by 26% .

The Bank’s deputy governor for financial stability, Sarah Breeden, said it was important to keep in mind that households would “face this [mortgage] shock with strong balance sheets”.

She said household debt was relatively low, at a level last seen in the early 2000s. “So they start from a position of some resilience. And secondly … while there’s a distributional effect and some households would be hit more than others, in aggregate we think this is absorbable.”

The Bank also raised concerns on Thursday about cybersecurity and AI threats after recent outages at Google and Microsoft laid bare businesses’ growing dependence on outside technology, and how “disruption at a single provider” could “affect many firms at once”.

The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, told a press conference that policymakers were worried about “open weight” AI – open source models, many of which are being developed in China. “These models can be run more cheaply … Safeguards may be disabled or removed more easily. This could make more advanced AI capabilities more readily available and useful to malicious actors,” he said.

The Bank also raised fears for the first time about emerging quantum computing capabilities potentially undermining the encryption technology that protects essential financial transactions.

Bailey said quantum computing would have been at the top of everyone’s mind this year, but that the surprise development of frontier AI models had overshadowed those concerns.

“It’s slightly moved quantum into the background … as you can see, we are very intentionally saying we can’t forget about quantum computing, it’s still coming down the track,” he said.

He emphasised that it was crucial, and possible, for banks to start to build up their defences against quantum risks, even while the technology was in nascent development. “It could have powers that go beyond what we’re seeing with frontier AI and have substantial power to undermine cryptography,” he said.

The Bank said the evolving risks reinforced the need for “significant and sustained investment by the financial sector in building resilience”, adding that banks needed to have credible arrangements to ensure they could bounce back quickly from any disruption and maintain “vital financial services”.

The financial policy committee acknowledged this would place competing demands on lenders’ tech experts and management teams, but added that a failure to take action would “compromise firms’ operational resilience with potential system-wide implications”.

The Bank also announced plans on Thursday to further reduce capital requirements for UK banks, as part of a wider package that it said could unleash an extra £175bn in lending capacity. However, extra funding could end up being used to pay out shareholders and investors.

Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffs

Published 25 November 2026

The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%.

The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.

The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.

Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.

The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.

The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".

Jamieson Greer, US trade representative

He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression".

They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said.

But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.

Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.

Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.

Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.

Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year

These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said.

Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said.

The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said.

Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration.

However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.

"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.

The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added.

Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move.

Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers.

Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade.

The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US.

"Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said.

The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.

The latest tariff rate is "not consistent" with the reality of bilateral economic-trade cooperation between the US and Vietnam, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Bui Thanh Son said.

The Japanese government said the US tariffs were "regrettable", while the Singapore government said it disagrees with the White House's findings and that it is engaging the USTR to explore ways to reduce the tariff.

South Korea's trade minister said the proposed 15% tariff will be "more than a decent outcome" as it would fall in line with a previously agreed limit with Washington.

Last year, Seoul pledged $350bn (£267bn) in US investments in exchange for lower tariffs as part of a trade deal.

Trump tariffs on Asia: Which economies were hit hardest? Published 1 August 2025

China's growth accelerates as AI boom helps boost exports Published 19 October

US trading partners have been "waiting for this shoe to drop" and have argued that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's Wendy Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.

"Many believe that China, not them, should be the target for US action," she added.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun described the new tariffs as a form of "political manipulation", describing as "false" the US claim that China produces more than it can consume.

The tariff announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.

The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.

Beijing has remained vague on how it will respond but for now seems "prepared to live with the new rates provided they don't exceed 20%", Cutler said.

Most people who play video games can spend hours enjoying them without experiencing any problems. But for a small minority, gaming becomes so important that relationships, education or work begin to suffer. How can we tell when enthusiasm has become a disorder?

In 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) formally recognised gaming disorder in its International Classification of Diseases. It describes a persistent pattern in which someone loses control over gaming , gives it priority over other activities and continues playing despite harmful consequences. For a diagnosis, the behaviour must seriously affect everyday life, usually for at least 12 months.

The diagnosis has prompted debate. Gaming brings enjoyment and social connection to millions of people, and researchers disagree about where intense involvement ends and a clinical problem begins.

In 2013, the American Psychiatric Association included “internet gaming disorder” in its diagnostic manual. However, it classified it as a condition requiring further study rather than an established diagnosis. The WHO subsequently adopted its own diagnostic criteria for gaming disorder.

I have researched problematic gaming for decades, beginning with work examining similarities between video games and slot machines . Researchers use terms such as “excessive gaming”, “problematic gaming” and “gaming addiction”, sometimes interchangeably. I regard addiction as the extreme end of a spectrum of gaming-related difficulties. The crucial question is whether someone is losing control and experiencing harm.

Why some people are more vulnerable

In a review of research , my colleagues and I examined what may contribute to the development of gaming disorder. We found that no single factor explains it. Personality, motivations for playing, mental health, biological differences and the design of games can all play a part.

Research has repeatedly found an association between gaming disorder and a personality trait known as neuroticism. People with higher levels of neuroticism tend to be more sensitive to stress and more prone to negative emotions.

People who experience more anxiety or distress may find virtual worlds reassuring or easier to control than their everyday circumstances. Gaming can offer temporary relief, but relying on it to escape difficulties may become problematic.

Gaming disorder has been linked to depression and anxiety . Research also suggests that people with ADHD or autism may be more likely to develop problems with gaming. Some studies have found a link between problematic gaming and suicidal thoughts , although this does not mean that gaming causes them.

However, much of this research on mental health examines people’s gaming habits and mental health at a single point in time. We cannot assume that gaming causes these difficulties, or that they necessarily cause gaming disorder. The relationship may work in both directions.

Studies using brain scans have identified differences in the brains of some people with problematic gaming. These differences occur in areas involved in how people respond to rewards, make decisions and control their behaviour.

Similar findings have been reported in research on other addictions. However, we cannot tell from these studies whether the brain differences existed before the gaming problems began or developed alongside them.

The games people choose may also matter. “Massively multiplayer online role-playing games” have frequently been associated with problematic gaming . In these games, large numbers of players share a virtual world that continues to exist even when they log off.

Researchers have also identified links with shooting and strategy games. But games vary considerably, as do the people who play them. A game’s genre alone does not make it addictive.

Game design can encourage repeated play through challenges, achievements and rewards. Some rewards arrive unpredictably, giving players a reason to try again because the next attempt might bring something valuable.

Psychologists call one form of this “variable-ratio reinforcement”. Players receive rewards but cannot predict how many attempts it will take to earn them. Such reward systems can help explain why some players find it difficult to stop, although their effects differ from person to person.

There are also concerns about how some games make money. Some games offer microtransactions, which allow players to spend real money on items or features within the game. These include loot boxes, which provide random virtual rewards without players knowing exactly what they will receive. The resemblance to gambling has attracted particular attention because loot boxes can be available to children.

A systematic review of research found associations between spending on loot boxes and both problematic gambling and gaming. However, this evidence does not establish that buying loot boxes causes either condition. Nor does it establish that buying loot boxes leads people into gambling later.

When should someone seek help?

One warning sign is being unable to cut back on gaming despite repeated attempts. Others include withdrawing from relationships or losing interest in other activities. Some people continue playing even when gaming is seriously affecting their work or education.

Some people become irritable or anxious when they cannot play, or conceal how much time they spend gaming. No single warning sign is enough to diagnose gaming disorder, but ongoing problems deserve attention.

If gaming is taking over someone’s life, they can seek help from a GP or mental health professional. These professionals can help assess the problem and determine whether specialist support is needed.

In England, the NHS also has a National Centre for Gaming Disorders , which provides specialist support for people aged 13 and over.

It is equally important to remember that many people play for long periods without suffering any harm. As I have argued throughout my research, the difference between a healthy enthusiasm and an addiction is that one adds to life while the other takes away from it.

stories.body:
Les efforts de lutte contre le paludisme et d’élimination de la maladie au sein de la Communauté de développement de l’Afrique australe (SADC) se trouvent à un point critique . Au cours des deux dernières années, le nombre de cas a augmenté dans la région. Plusieurs pays ont enregistré un recul des progrès durement acquis. Les populations vivant dans des zones à risque de paludisme sont désormais davantage exposées qu’auparavant.

Quatre pays de la région – la République démocratique du Congo, le Mozambique, l’Angola et la Tanzanie – figurent parmi ceux qui sont les plus touchés par le paludisme au monde. Ce classement est établi en fonction du nombre de nouveaux cas de paludisme pour 1 000 personnes exposées au risque chaque année. À eux quatre, ces pays représentent 22,9 % de la charge mondiale du paludisme.

L’objectif fixé par l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) d'éliminer le paludisme d’ici à 2030 est désormais plus difficile à atteindre.

Remettre la région de la SADC sur la bonne voie nécessitera des efforts considérables et une mobilisation collective. Plusieurs menaces se conjuguent dans la région et exigent chacune des réponses rapides et efficaces.

Les programmes nationaux de lutte contre le paludisme sont débordés et manquent de ressources. L’imprévisibilité et l’évolution constante du paysage mondial du financement de la santé aggravent encore la situation. Les programmes africains de lutte contre le paludisme ont longtemps reposé sur les financements des bailleurs de fonds. L’Afrique du Sud fait figure d’exception : elle finance la quasi-totalité de son programme national.

Je dirige le Laboratoire de surveillance de la résistance aux antipaludiques et de recherche opérationnelle sur le paludisme de l'Institut national sud-africain des maladies transmissibles . Nous surveillons la résistance aux médicaments antipaludiques dans les districts où le paludisme est endémique, en Afrique du Sud et dans les pays voisins.

Au vu de nos observations, je pense que les gouvernements africains devraient investir davantage dans la lutte contre le paludisme et son élimination dans leurs pays respectifs.

Les phénomènes météorologiques extrêmes sont également devenus plus fréquents dans la région, augmentant ainsi le risque de propagation des maladies infectieuses. Les pays doivent s’y préparer et élaborer des plans pour en atténuer les conséquences.

À ces difficultés s’ajoute la persistance de la résistance aux médicaments antipaludiques et aux insecticides. Les traitements sont moins efficaces qu’auparavant, car les parasites ont développé des mécanismes de résistance. La région a besoin de pôles de génomique capables de surveiller la manière dont les parasites réagissent aux mesures de prévention et aux traitements.

Réductions des financements

La suspension brutale, en 2025 , du financement du gouvernement américain destiné à soutenir des activités essentielles de lutte contre le paludisme a compliqué les efforts du Fonds mondial pour atteindre son objectif de reconstitution de 18 milliards de dollars américains au titre de son 8e cycle de financements .

Tous les trois ans, les pays du monde entier sont invités à apporter des contributions au Fonds mondial de lutte contre le sida, la tuberculose et le paludisme.

Les dotations allouées aux pays pour le cycle de subventions 2026-2028 sont en moyenne inférieures de 18 % à celles du cycle précédent. Les pays bénéficiaires doivent donc faire des choix difficiles : déterminer quelles populations protéger, quels moyens mettre en œuvre et quelles zones géographiques cibler. Il n’est désormais plus possible d’intervenir partout et auprès de tout le monde.

À cela s’ajoute la nécessité de réduire certaines activités, telles que la distribution de moustiquaires imprégnées d’insecticide, la réalisation d’enquêtes sur les indicateurs du paludisme et l’administration de médicaments à titre préventif. Les interventions dont l’efficacité est avérée et qui visent à protéger les populations les plus vulnérables et les plus exposées au risque de paludisme sont privilégiées, au détriment de celles jugées moins rentables. Cette priorisation laisse certaines populations moins vulnérables moins bien protégées. De plus, le financement des activités visant à éliminer le paludisme n’est plus prioritaire.

En conséquence, le nombre de cas de paludisme a augmenté a augmenté dans plusieurs pays, notamment au Mozambique, au Nigeria et en Ouganda.

Ces changements soudains et imprévus dans les priorités des bailleurs de fonds mettent en évidence la vulnérabilité des programmes nationaux de lutte contre le paludisme. Ceux-ci dépendent excessivement de l’aide extérieure pour financer leurs activités essentielles.

Impact du changement climatique

Le phénomène climatique La Niña, qui s'est manifesté au début début 2026, a provoqué de graves inondations dans plusieurs pays de la SADC.

Il a endommagé des infrastructures essentielles, provoquant le déplacement de communautés locales. Ces inondations ont endommagé des infrastructures essentielles et entraîné le déplacement de communautés locales. Elles ont également contribué à une augmentation du nombre de cas de paludisme dans plusieurs pays, notamment au Zimbabwe , au Mozambique et en Afrique du Sud .

Le Mozambique a enregistré une augmentation de 55 % du nombre de cas de paludisme au cours des six premières semaines de 2026, par rapport à la même période en 2025.

Au Zimbabwe, 65 399 cas ont été signalés au premier trimestre 2026, soit près du double du nombre enregistré au cours de la même période en 2025.

Les populations déplacées, comme les personnes mobiles et migrantes de la région, franchissent fréquemment les frontières pour accéder à des services essentiels dans les pays ou les régions voisins. Ces déplacements accentuent la pression sur des établissements de santé déjà surchargés et augmentent le risque de rupture de stock de médicaments.

En 2025, l’Organisation internationale pour les migrations et le Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies pour les réfugiés ont estimé à environ 11,4 millions le nombre de personnes déplacées de force dans la région de la SADC, soit une hausse de 35 % par rapport à 2023.

Tous les pays de la SADC doivent se doter de systèmes d’alerte précoce efficaces et de plans d’intervention pour faire face aux phénomènes météorologiques extrêmes, aux arrivées imprévues de personnes déplacées et à la recrudescence des maladies infectieuses. Ces dispositifs doivent reposer sur un partage rapide des données, ainsi que sur une coordination et une coopération renforcées à l’échelle régionale.

Alors que le phénomène climatique de « super El Niño » devrait provoquer des conditions chaudes et sèches en Afrique australe, de fortes précipitations et des inondations sont attendues en Afrique de l’Est et centrale . Cette situation pourrait entraîner une augmentation du nombre de personnes déplacées et favoriser la propagation de maladies dans la région de la SADC. Dans ce contexte, il est essentiel de disposer de plans régionaux de préparation et d’intervention dotés de financements suffisants et reposant sur des mécanismes de coordination efficaces.

Des défis persistants

Des scientifiques ont confirmé que, dans certaines régions, les traitements recommandés contre le paludisme sont devenus moins efficaces qu’auparavant, en raison de mutations génétiques du parasite responsable de la maladie. Or, tous les pays de la SADC ne disposent pas des capacités nécessaires pour détecter et analyser ces mutations.

La création de pôles régionaux de surveillance génomique permettrait de repérer rapidement les signes émergents de résistance aux traitements. Sans une telle surveillance proactive, le risque de propagation de souches résistantes aux médicaments et d'augmentation de la mortalité liée au paludisme pourrait s'accroître.

Malgré plusieurs initiatives de formation, comme le programme de bourses en entomologie E8 , les entomologistes qualifiés (scientifiques spécialisés dans l’étude des insectes) restent peu nombreux au sein des programmes nationaux de lutte contre le paludisme. Cette pénurie limite les capacités de surveillance des populations de moustiques et de détection d’une éventuelle résistance aux insecticides. Elle complique également le choix des stratégies de lutte antivectorielle les plus appropriées, fondées sur les données disponibles.

Dans un contexte de ressources limitées, le lancement de nouveaux programmes de formation constituera un véritable défi.

Se remettre sur la bonne voie

Si la région de la SADC s’est engagée à éliminer le paludisme d’ici à 2030 , les financements nationaux doivent permettre de combler les lacunes en matière d’intervention et de soutenir les activités d’élimination essentielles. Si rien n’est fait, le nombre de cas augmentera probablement dans certaines zones et au sein de certaines populations.

Les pays devraient envisager de mobiliser les spécialistes des moustiques déjà présents dans la région afin de favoriser les échanges d’expériences entre pairs et le renforcement des capacités. Les centres de surveillance génomique mis en place pour détecter la résistance aux médicaments pourraient également contribuer au suivi de la résistance aux insecticides à l’échelle régionale.

Le degré élevé d’interconnexion entre les pays de la région, conjugué à la réduction des budgets consacrés à la santé, montre que l’élimination du paludisme ne pourra être atteinte sans une collaboration et une coordination régionales durables.
